**This cluster covers the subject of the article's strongest conclusion**, that pure thrust vectoring cannot meet a crosswind landing requirement. It holds crosswind technique, approach and landing handling qualities, automatic and carrier landing, wind shear on approach, and landing rollout directional control.

### Wings, aerofoils and flow control

**The wing outside the delta and supersonic clusters.** Aerofoil and wing aerodynamics, boundary layers and transition, wingtip devices, high lift and active flow control. **The X-44A's deep, inversely cambered wing is a subject of this literature rather than of the delta cluster.**

## Where the Framing Breaks Down

**Five places, and only the first of them is quantified here.**

**The ratio treats jet velocity as constant across the envelope, which it is not. Relaxing that assumption moves the answer in the article's favour.** Carrying the jet velocity relation through the ratio gives

$$\mathcal{R}(M) \propto \frac{\eta_{r}(M) \left( 1 + 0.2 M^{2} \right)^{3} V_{j}(M)}{M^{2}}$$

and at an overall engine pressure ratio of eight the jet velocity rises by **25.7 percent** from the approach to Mach 2.25, which is far from constant.

| | minimising Mach | demonstrated point above the worst case |
|---|---|---|
| constant jet velocity | 1.674 | 1.135 |
| varying jet velocity | 1.550 | 1.078 |

**The minimum moves forward and gets shallower, so the demonstrated point stands 7.8 percent above the worst supersonic condition rather than 13.5.** The conclusion drawn from the pessimistic assumption survives the correction and improves. **The result is also robust to the one engine parameter it introduces.** Across overall pressure ratios from four to twenty the minimising Mach moves only from 1.502 to 1.589 and the penalty from 5.9 to 9.5 percent.

**What the correction does change is the top of the envelope.** Under the constant assumption Mach 2.0 and Mach 2.25 were harder than the demonstrated point. With the jet velocity varying they are easier, at 1.006 and 1.103 times, so the high supersonic end stops being a concern. **The minimum's existence never depended on the assumption, because it comes from the mass flow term, and only its location and depth did.**

**A second approximation remains unquantified and runs the other way.** The relation above assumes the afterburner is lit, and a dry-thrust case has a lower total temperature and a lower jet velocity, which would make those conditions less favourable than any table here. **This article does not compute the dry case, and the envelope should not be read as covered.**

**The engine-out identity assumes the vectoring is available on the live engine at full deflection.** A nozzle that has failed for the same reason the engine has failed provides nothing, and a common-cause failure of an engine and its nozzle is a case a fin covers and a nozzle does not. **The argument belongs to reliability engineering, outside aerodynamics, and no quantitative form of it is attempted.**

**Treating the two vehicles in one article follows from the designation, and engineering supplies no reason for it.** They share a contractor, a decade and a number. They share no requirement, no size class, no speed range and no mission. **A reader interested in either aeroplane is being handed a good deal of material about a different one**, justified because the collision is the subject.

**The crosswind case assumes the aeroplane must land in a crosswind on a runway.** A vehicle that lands into wind on a long runway at a test range faces a much weaker requirement than an operational fighter does, and the MANTA as an X-plane would have been the former. **The impossibility derived above is a statement about the operational aeroplane the MANTA was a step toward, not necessarily about the demonstrator**, and the distinction holds even though every published description of the MANTA frames it as a step toward a fighter.

## The Source Base

**The argument in this article rests on nine documents and the rest of the reference list is a map of the surrounding literature.**

**Two carry the flight result.** The X-31 quasi-tailless demonstration description \[[Huber and Schellenger 1994][research_huberpeter_schellengerharveyg_1994]\] and the flight test results report \[[Bosworth and Stoliker 1996][research_bosworthjohnt_stolikerpc_1996]\] supply the flight condition, the technique, the manoeuvres and the conclusion. **Everything this article says about what has actually been demonstrated comes from these two.**

**One carries the nozzle.** The measurement of multiaxis control power from a two-dimensional convergent-divergent nozzle with sidewall yaw flaps across Mach 0.20 to 2.47 \[[Capone and Bare 1987][research_caponefrancisj_bareeann_1987]\] is the evidence that the hardware the MANTA needed can be built and characterised.

**One carries the alternative.** The study of differential canard deflection as a yaw generator on the X-31 with and without its vertical tail \[[Whiting 1996][research_whitingmatthewrobert_1996]\] establishes that an aerodynamic yaw effector of comparable authority to the vectoring vanes was studied on the same aeroplane, which is what makes the low-speed conclusion above a design choice rather than a dead end.

**Five carry the vehicles themselves and none of them is a primary document.** The MANTA and unmanned X-44A encyclopaedia entries \[[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA][ref_x44_manta_wikipedia]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-44, the unmanned vehicle][ref_x44_uav_wikipedia]\], the journalism that broke the story \[[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]\] \[[Skunk Works reveals the missing link in a secret unmanned history][ref_flightglobal_x44a]\], and the museum fact sheet \[[Lockheed Martin X-44A, National Museum of the United States Air Force][ref_x44a_museum]\] are the core of the public record on these two aircraft, which the 2003 NASA inventory of X-vehicles \[[Jenkins, Landis and Miller, American X-Vehicles, An Inventory X-1 to X-50, NASA SP-2003-4531, 2003][ref_american_x_vehicles]\] and two secondary compilations \[[X-44 MANTA Multi-Axis No-Tail Aircraft, GlobalSecurity][ref_globalsecurity_x44]\] \[[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA tailless technology demonstrator proposal][ref_militaryfactory_x44]\] supplement. **That is a thin foundation and the article is built to survive it**, which is why the analysis of the MANTA rests on the F-22's published numbers and the X-31's published flight results, and why the one X-44A result is stated as a bound on the museum's figures.

**Two sources are used with a stated reservation.** The two National Museum of the United States Air Force pages return a Hypertext Transfer Protocol status of 403 to automated requests, which is bot mitigation and not absence. **Both were read through copies held by the Internet Archive**, since neither could be read directly from the museum's own site.

**The research survey holds 9,631 records, of which 9,182 resolve through Crossref digital object identifiers and 449 through NASA's Technical Reports Server.** **The median publication year is 2005.** Of the 9,429 dated records, 706 were published before 1970, being 7.5 percent, and 3,128 in 2015 or later, being 33.5 percent.

**Counting a displayed relation as cited when the paragraph next before or after it carries a citation, 45 of the article's 59 displayed relations carry none.** That gap remains open.

### The Definition of Primary

**Primacy is a property of the document, and this survey derives it from the identifier.** A record is primary when it comes from NASA's Technical Reports Server or carries a Defense Technical Information Center, American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, SAE International or Office of Scientific and Technical Information identifier, and it is a report primary when it is a NASA or Defense Technical Information Center record. **By that rule 5,625 of the 9,631 research records are primary, being 58.4 percent, and 1,317 are report primaries, being 13.7 percent.** **That second figure matters most**, because the relations this article displays were established in report series that a search of journals and conferences cannot see at all.

**Eleven foundational primaries carry relations this article displays**, and a search returning something adjacent would be worse than useless for any of them. They are Munk on the aerodynamic forces on airship hulls, Multhopp on the aerodynamics of the fuselage, Allen and Perkins on viscous flow over slender inclined bodies, Oswald on the calculation of airplane performance, the U.S. Standard Atmosphere, Gilruth on requirements for satisfactory flying qualities, Campbell and McKinney and Toll and Queijo and Jones and Alksne on lateral derivative estimation, and two in-flight evaluations of pure control system time delays. **Every one is cited in the prose beside the relation it establishes rather than only in the reference list.**

### Thin Subjects

**The subjects the derivations rest on are well covered when asked for in the field's own vocabulary**, which speaks of directional stability and control, the vertical tail, the empennage and lateral-directional characteristics rather than of tail sizing. Counting the research titles that match a fixed pattern for each subject, and counting as a report primary a record from NASA's Technical Reports Server or the Defense Technical Information Center, vertical tail sizing and the directional requirement returns 218 records with 35 report primaries, the slender-body fuselage contribution 252, the drag polar and span efficiency 51, and loop bandwidth with transport delay 38.

**Four subjects that this article's derivations depend on have thin literatures.** Each count below is the number of research records in this survey whose title carries at least one of the listed terms.

| Subject | Title terms counted | Records |
|---|---|---|
| the standard atmosphere | standard atmosphere, atmospheric model, density, pressure, temperature or properties, tropopause, altitude variation or effect on density or pressure | 2 |
| wing internal volume and fuel | fuel volume, tank, capacity, fraction, system or load, internal volume, wing volume, tankage or thickness, volumetric, thickness ratio | 3 |
| thrust lapse and the corrected-flow model | corrected flow, mass, airflow, parameter, speed or weight flow, thrust lapse, lapse rate, thrust variation or change with altitude, Mach or speed, engine performance at altitude | 2 |
| quasi-tailless technique and in-flight simulation | quasi tailless, in-flight simulation, variable stability, simulated tail or instability, tail off simulation, airborne simulator | 21 |

**Each is thin for one of the three recognised reasons.** The standard atmosphere returns two records, both of them the standard tables themselves, because it is **so settled that it stopped generating papers** and became a standards document instead, which is cited as one. Wing internal volume returns three records and none of them concerns how much volume a wing encloses, two being composite structures that carry a fuel tank and the other the aerodynamics of wing thickness, because **that relation lives in design textbooks and not in the report literature**, and it is cited to books accordingly. Thrust lapse and the corrected-flow model return two records, both on matching engine and aircraft lapse rates for a high-speed civil transport, for the same reason, and the article takes that model from propulsion texts and calibrates the lapse exponent itself. Quasi-tailless technique and in-flight simulation returns twenty-one records with eleven report primaries, and **it is small because the field is small**, one aeroplane having flown the experiment inside a variable-stability tradition that is itself narrow. **Naming which kind each one is matters more than the counts**, because none of the four is a gap that searching could close.

**The subject of this article's framing cannot be surveyed by bibliographic search at all.** The survey holds no cluster on designation practice, because designation, classification, records, identifier and secrecy are among the least discriminating words in any literature, and the nine research titles in it that carry designation or nomenclature use those words for propulsion station numbering, aerodynamic and aircraft nomenclature, aerofoil series and a company project number. **No title in the survey names the X-44 or the MANTA.** **That is a fourth kind of thin beyond the three the series recognises**, and the real sources for the subject are the designation registries themselves, which this article cites in the Reference category and quotes in the section on the two referents.

### What the Survey Admits

**A record is admitted only when a person reading its title finds it on this article's subject.** The subject is directional stability and control and the vertical tail, tailless and flying-wing aircraft, thrust vectoring, exhaust nozzles, engine cycle and inlet performance, delta and swept wing, supersonic and slender-body aerodynamics, flight control, handling qualities, approach and landing, low observability and survivability, aircraft design and performance, unmanned aircraft as aircraft and as military systems, airframe structure and manufacture, wind tunnel and flight test and air data, the atmosphere as the flight condition, engine failure, and aircraft programmes and their history. Every record is filed under a named literature, and the survey has no residual cluster.

**Many words this subject depends on also name something else, and a record that shares only such a word or a distant application is excluded.** Yaw, roll, rudder and autopilot also belong to ship steering, yaw, sideslip and torque vectoring to road vehicle dynamics, crosswind and the wind tunnel to civil wind engineering and railway aerodynamics, and wing, flight, lift and drag to the flight of insects, birds and bats. Nozzle also names the cavitating nozzles of hydraulics and the process nozzles of steam, refrigerants and powder atomisation, the pilot stage of a hydraulic valve is not a person, the blended wing body is an underwater vehicle configuration in the identical phrase, and aerofoils are also wind turbine blades. Unmanned vehicles also run on the ground and on the sea surface and serve agriculture, mapping and inspection, fighter also names the fire fighter, reconnaissance also has its ground military senses, radar cross section is also measured on ships, and spacecraft trajectories and drag reduction in water have literatures of their own. **Aeronautical subjects that the argument does not use are excluded as well**, among them icing, aircraft noise and the sonic boom, rotorcraft, airline and airport operations, air traffic management, aircraft subsystems and maintenance, flutter, and the combustion, cooling and materials of gas turbines.

**Records that are not works are excluded as well.** Crossref registers peer reviews as records whose titles read as a review of a named paper and supplementary files as components sharing an identifier stem with their parent, and military part specifications carry titles that are noun phrases inverted for filing. Corrections, errata, retractions, withdrawals, figures, supplementary material, peer-review reports, front matter, whole conference volumes that state no subject, and standards for parts, materials, test methods and documentation are parts of works, editorial events or specifications rather than works. Reviews of books, dictionary and other reference entries of two pages or fewer, news and other notices, and a second deposit of a document already in the survey are not admitted either, while an authored encyclopedia article of more than two pages and a textbook chapter are research works and stay. **None of these makes a claim, so none is counted.**

**Some records of doubtful relevance are kept**, among them rocket, missile and spacecraft thrust vector control, the radar and infrared signature of rotorcraft, the directional stability of birds and the yaw control of flapping flyers, which need no vertical tail, aircraft designed for Mars, gust load alleviation, and control theory that names time delay, actuator saturation or control allocation without naming an aircraft. Each shares a mechanism, a configuration question or a relation with this subject, and a reader may weigh it accordingly.

**Every research title has been read for relevance, so the off-topic share that remains is a matter of reading judgement.**

## Epistemic State

### Historical Fact

**The X-44 MANTA was a Lockheed Martin design study of a tailless F-22 derivative controlled by three-axis thrust vectoring.** Preliminary work was under way by May 1999 and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration approved a programme start in June 1999. No aircraft was built.

**The X-44A unmanned aircraft was built by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works in 1999 and first flew in 2001.** It has a span of about 30 feet, is powered by a Williams F112, was first reported in February 2018 and was publicly unveiled in March 2018. It has been displayed at the National Museum of the United States Air Force since October 2020.

**The X-31 flew a quasi-tailless flight demonstration beginning in March 1994**, at Mach 1.2 and 37,500 feet with a simulated one hundred percent vertical tail reduction, and its report concludes that tailless and reduced-tail fighters are feasible when the capability is designed in from the start.

**The F-22's F119 nozzles vector in pitch only, through plus or minus twenty degrees.**

**The DarkStar was terminated in January 1999 and the Polecat first flew in 2005.**

### Verified by Independent Derivation

**The identity $q = 0.7 p M^{2}$ agrees with the density form at every flight condition used**, to one part in a million or better.

**The cancellation of static pressure from the authority ratio holds numerically at five altitudes above the tropopause**, to one part in ten to the twelfth, and the closed form agrees exactly with the full atmosphere model at three further altitudes.

**The minimum of the ideal Mach function at $M = \sqrt{5/2}$ and its value of exactly 1.35 are recovered by bisection on a numerically differenced derivative**, to six decimal places, independently of the algebra that produced them.

**The maximum of the crosswind function at exactly Mach one is recovered by golden-section search** to six decimal places, and the altitude independence holds at five altitudes to four parts in ten thousand, the residue being the small-angle approximation to the arctangent.

**The engine-out relation $\tan \delta = y/\ell$ is recovered by solving the moment balance numerically without cancelling the thrust**, at four thrusts spanning three orders of magnitude, agreeing to one part in a billion.

**The two expressions for the best lift to drag ratio agree to machine precision.** This tests transcription, since at the best ratio the induced drag equals the zero-lift drag exactly and the two forms are the same statement.

**The demand-over-availability ratio was derived a second time from the propulsive tail volume by a route that shares nothing with the first**, and reproduces the throttle factor of 5.33 to three significant figures.

**The remaining derived values can be recomputed from the relations shown**, among them the rudder baseline, the crosswind maximum, the small-angle error and its variation, the gearing, the loop budget, the slender-body inversion, the quasi-tailless gearing, the drag polar and the varying jet velocity.

### Analysis

**The ratio of thrust-vectored yaw authority to aerodynamic yaw demand is independent of pressure altitude and, above the tropopause, a function of Mach number alone.** This follows from static pressure entering the engine mass flow and the dynamic pressure to the same power.

**That function has a minimum at Mach 1.581 with ideal recovery and Mach 1.674 with a military specification inlet recovery model.** The X-31's demonstrated point at Mach 1.2 stands 1.135 times above the second, and no point from Mach 1.2 to Mach 2.25 is more than twelve percent harder than what was flown.

**For a crosswind of fixed speed, the required vector angle depends on Mach number alone and peaks at exactly Mach one.** Pressure and temperature both cancel.

**Restoring the demonstrated margin on a sea-level approach at 150 knots in a 15 metre per second crosswind requires 38.4 percent throttle against the 7.2 percent the glide slope needs at an assumed landing ratio of six, a factor of 5.33, or against 12.4 percent at the ratio of about four measured on a straight-wing fighter, a factor of 3.09.** The implied lift to drag ratio in level flight at that thrust is between 1.6 and 1.9, below the lowest effective ratio of 2.7 flown in the low lift to drag landing research.

**The directional divergence of a tailless F-22 has a time to double between 0.16 and 0.91 seconds across a wide bracket of the two unpublished quantities it depends on**, and the entire supersonic column of that bracket is below four tenths of a second.

**A thrust lapse exponent of 0.960 in density ratio reproduces the DarkStar's published ceiling, weight and thrust** on an assumed 42 square metre wing, an Oswald efficiency of 0.85 and a zero-lift drag coefficient of 0.015.

**Primary sources stand at 5,625 of 9,631 research records, or 58.4 percent, and report primaries alone at 1,317 or 13.7 percent.** Records from 2015 or later number 3,128, or 33.5 percent of those dated, and 705 records predate 1970.

**Relaxing the constant jet velocity assumption moves the minimising Mach from 1.674 to 1.550 and cuts the demonstrated point's penalty from 13.5 percent to 7.8**, so the conclusion drawn under the pessimistic assumption survives its own correction and improves. Across engine pressure ratios from four to twenty the minimising Mach moves only from 1.502 to 1.589.

**Expressed as a propulsive tail volume, the vectoring supplies 0.0181 at the demonstration point against about 0.0412 for thirty degrees of a conventional rudder**, or 44 percent, and 5.19 times as much at maximum thrust on approach. **The same quantity collapses to 0.0154 at glide-slope thrust**, which is the throttle result arrived at from the other direction.

**The stabilisation loop must close within 60 to 90 milliseconds supersonically and 145 to 218 on approach**, from a crossover of two to three times the unstable pole and thirty degrees of phase margin budgeted to transport delay.

**Inverting the slender-body yawing moment for the fuselage volume that the assumed derivative implies gives 33.8 cubic metres, a mean cross-section of 1.79 square metres over the F-22's length.** No fuselage volume is published to compare with, and the two engine envelopes alone account for about a third of that volume, so **the instability bracket is reported as a bracket and not as a conservative bound.**

### Inference

**The MANTA required a nozzle capability the F-22 does not have**, since a two-dimensional convergent-divergent nozzle deflects only in the plane of its flaps. This is inferred from the published nozzle description, and one MANTA account states the requirement directly in giving the aircraft pitch and yaw vectoring nozzles \[[X-44 MANTA Multi-Axis No-Tail Aircraft, GlobalSecurity][ref_globalsecurity_x44]\].

**Pure thrust vectoring cannot meet an operational crosswind landing requirement**, so a tailless fighter needs an aerodynamic yaw effector that works at low speed. The throttle calculation supports this inference, which is consistent with the X-36's split ailerons and with the X-31 differential canard study, neither of which is offered as confirmation.

**The X-44A's wing loading is at most about twice the DarkStar's, and below it if the aircraft cruised above about 23,000 feet**, an inference from the museum's speeds and an assumed drag polar and aspect ratio common to both. A cruise at a reconnaissance ceiling would need about twice the published maximum speed.

**The X-44A's published maximum speed is not a thrust limit on a clean polar**, since the engine makes about five times the clean drag at the bound, so either the drag was several times higher or another limit set the maximum.

**The X-44A was a short-range configuration and manufacturing demonstrator and not an endurance aircraft.** The published endurance and range indicate it, and the stated programme objectives agree.

**The stabilisation loop should be machinery rather than a pilot**, inferred from the delay budget and the phase margin it reserves. The divergence rate alone is within what practised subjects held in single-axis tracking.

**The difficulty in sensing sideslip is dynamic.** Writing the relation down gives a gearing near unity and a cost of 2.9 percent of available authority for a half-degree measurement error, which is not a hard requirement. **What binds is lag and noise at a crossover of six to nine radians per second.**

### What the Record Does Not Settle

**Whether the designation X-44A was ever officially assigned to either vehicle, and if to one, to which.** Both are recorded under it in the general reference literature. The specialist designation registry carries no page for the number at all. No allocation document has been published.

**Whether the two programmes had any relationship.** The journalism that revealed the unmanned aircraft states that it is unclear how it came to carry the designation and that there appears to be no direct relation. **An absence of known relation is not a known absence of relation.**

**When the MANTA was cancelled.** The sources place the end of funding in 2000 or around that year, a 2003 NASA inventory still describes a feasibility study in progress, and none cites a programme document.

**Everything about the X-44A's flight programme beyond the year of first flight and the museum's summary figures.** Number of flights, duration, envelope, instrumentation, results, and whether the aircraft in the museum is the only one built.

**Every specification of the MANTA.** Wing area, sweep, weights, required vector angles, control law architecture and the intended sideslip sensing. One reference site lists weights and performance for the MANTA without citing a source \[[Lockheed Martin X-44 MANTA tailless technology demonstrator proposal][ref_militaryfactory_x44]\].

**Whether the MANTA influenced any later programme.** No source cited here documents a connection to any later programme, and the sixth-generation fighter studies in the survey do not name it.

**The DarkStar's wing area**, which this article assumes because no source used publishes it, and on which the thrust lapse calibration and every number in the X-44A table depend, and the X-44A's aspect ratio, which this article takes from the DarkStar's.

### On Sources Used With Reservation

**The two National Museum of the United States Air Force pages refuse automated requests**, for the reason given in the Source Base, **and both were read through copies held by the Internet Archive.**

**The general encyclopaedia is the source for the MANTA's origin dates, its designation and its F-22 derivation, and one journalistic account reports the X-44A's nano-carbon fibre skin, which a second describes as an all carbon fibre airframe.** No primary document for any of those claims has been located, and the X-44A's engine, performance figures and museum placement rest on the museum fact sheet. The X-44A bound rests on the museum's performance figures, and none of the article's other results depends on these sources.

**Three secondary aviation outlets are cited for the X-44A's revelation and description** \[[Lockheed Skunk Works X-44A flying-wing drone revealed][ref_twz_x44a]\] \[[Skunk Works reveals the missing link in a secret unmanned history][ref_flightglobal_x44a]\] \[[Skunk Works reveals stealthy UAV demonstrator][ref_ain_x44a]\]. Beside the museum they are the only sources that have published on the aircraft in any detail, they are consistent with each other, and one of them states plainly what it does not know, which is a reason to trust it more.

### On Information Postdating the Editorial Date

**This article carries an editorial date of 19 November 2025 and is written from knowledge current at the time of writing**, which includes the 2018 revelation and 2020 museum placement of the X-44A and the accounts published after them. **Later accounts are described as accounts and not as record.**

## Out of Scope

**Fluidic thrust vectoring**, which replaces mechanical deflection with a secondary injected flow and changes the weight and signature arguments without changing the momentum balance used above.

**The radar cross section calculation itself.** The argument takes as given that a vertical tail is a large contributor and does not compute it.

**The X-45, X-46 and X-47 unmanned combat air vehicle programmes**, which are the next articles in this series and which share the tailless configuration question with the X-44A while answering an entirely different requirement.

**Engine-out reliability and the common-cause failure of an engine with its nozzle**, named in the framing section as a case a fin covers and a nozzle does not.

**The manufacturing claim in any quantitative form**, since no mass, lay-up, tooling or cycle-time figure is available.

**The F-22's flight control system**, a large subject that bears on this one only through the nozzle.

## Conclusion

**The X-44 is one number attached to two aeroplanes that share a contractor and nothing else, and the register does not record the collision.**

**The aeroplane that never existed asked a question that had already been answered.** The X-31 flew a fully simulated tailless configuration at Mach 1.2 and 37,500 feet in 1994 and concluded that the configuration is feasible. **This article adds a measure of how much of the envelope that one point covered.** The answer needs no vehicle data. The static pressure cancels from the governing ratio, above the tropopause the ratio depends only on Mach number, the ratio has a minimum at Mach 1.674 with a realistic inlet, and the demonstrated point stands thirteen and a half percent above the worst case. **One supersonic point very nearly covered the supersonic envelope.**

**The concept fails at the runway instead.** For a crosswind of fixed speed both pressure and temperature cancel and the demand peaks at exactly Mach one, so at equal throttle the approach is the easiest case in the envelope. **The throttle is not equal.** Restoring the demonstrated margin on approach needs three to five times the thrust the glide slope needs, and absorbing that thrust in level flight implies a lift to drag ratio below two. **A tailless fighter therefore needs an aerodynamic yaw effector at low speed that it does not need supersonically**, the architecture the X-36 flew and the MANTA proposed to delete.

**The engine-out case, which is one of the two reasons fins are large, does not size a thrust-vectored aeroplane at all**, because the vector angle that trims it satisfies $\tan \delta = y/\ell$ and the thrust cancels identically. **Two classic fin-sizing cases, opposite answers, and reasoning from the fin would have got both wrong.**

**The aeroplane that did exist was built in the year its predecessor was cancelled and flew two years later, and almost nothing about it has been released.** The museum's figures, a maximum of 176 miles per hour, an hour and a half and 230 miles, describe a short-range demonstrator, and a cruise at a reconnaissance ceiling would have needed about twice that speed. **They bound its wing loading at no more than about twice the DarkStar's, and below the DarkStar's if it cruised above about 23,000 feet**, so the wing loading cannot say what the aircraft was for. **The endurance can, and it agrees with the programme's stated purpose of demonstrating a configuration and a factory.**

**The last observation concerns the designation instead of either aeroplane.** The X-planes sequence is a finite resource issued once and never replenished, and a number spent twice is still a number spent once. **The register carries no record of the ambiguity, the specialist directory carries no page for the number, and the encyclopaedia has resolved the collision by writing two articles and noting that they appear to be unrelated.** The cost of the confusion falls entirely on whoever reads the record later, which in this instance is this article.
